What Needs You
Search How This Works
Search
What Needs You
Show Everything

What Needs You is where the world tells you things and asks you things. A notice says what happened: groceries you couldn’t pay for, a commitment you slept through, a welcome to the school. A question carries its answers as buttons, such as File It or Keep The Account, and Dismiss. The number beside Home on the menu is how many of both are waiting.

Where To Find It
Home, The What Needs You Panel.
When You Can Use It
From “What Needs You”.
Show Me Where
What To Press
Open Home and read What Needs You: questions first, then notices.
Press one of a question’s answers to act on it there. It does what the same button on its own screen does.
Press Go There to open the screen a question or a notice is about.
Press Dismiss to take a question off the list without answering it.
Press Mark N Read, at the top of the panel, to mark every unread notice read at once.
Press Show All N, under the notices, to see every unread one before you do: the panel draws the six most important first, and Show The Six Most Important goes back to them.
Press a question’s or a notice’s title to open it: how urgent or important it is, when it closes, and where it sits in the list.

Sources And Estimates

Chase refuses to authorize any transaction once a card is reported lost or stolen, and sends a replacement card with a new number; for a credit card the account itself stays open and keeps its age for credit reporting.

Chase monitors cards around the clock and may contact the customer by text message, push notification, email or phone call to confirm whether unusual activity was authorized; fraud alerts are automatic and need no enrollment. Chase can refuse to authorize a transaction it reasonably believes may be fraudulent, but doesn’t say it holds a payment pending the customer's reply.

The law on the debit card: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6(b), a consumer who reports a lost or stolen debit card within two business days of learning of it owes at most the lesser of $50 or the transfers made before notice; after two business days the cap rises to $500. Transfers shown on a periodic statement that aren't reported within 60 days of the statement being sent carry unlimited liability for transfers after that 60-day window. The 2- and 60-day clocks run from different starts: learning of the loss, and the statement's transmittal.

The law on the credit card: Truth in Lending Act, Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.12(b)(1)(ii): a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card use is capped at the lesser of $50 or the amount obtained before the card issuer is notified.

The law on a payment you report as not yours: Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.11: the bank must decide within 10 business days (20 for a new account's first 30 days); if it takes longer it must provisionally credit the account within 10 business days and may take up to 45 days, or 90 days for point-of-sale debit card, out-of-state or new-account transfers. Results go to the consumer within 3 business days of finishing.
